passage: Placement cell note, by Aparna. Rukmini came to my office on Thursday, twelve days after her final interview at a logistics firm. The recruiter had told her, "You will hear from us by Friday." Nothing had come. She said she had been refreshing her inbox all week and had stopped preparing for other interviews. Her voice was tight, she kept twisting her lanyard, and she said quietly, "Maybe I wasn't good enough." I did not agree with that. We drafted one polite follow-up together and she sent it from my office. I suggested a second only if a week passes without an answer. I also asked her to apply to the two other openings on the notice board, so she is not waiting on one door. She left looking steadier. I will check in with her next week.

qa.q: How long after her final interview did Rukmini come to Aparna?
qa.a: She came twelve days after her final interview.

qa.q: What was Rukmini worried about, and what shows it?
qa.a: She feared she was not good enough. She said so quietly, and her tight voice and twisting lanyard show how anxious she was.

qa.q: What should Rukmini do after the follow-up?
qa.a: She can send a second polite message only if a week passes, keep applying to the other openings, and not read the silence as a verdict on her worth. 👍

qa.q: Why might the recruiter have gone silent without it being about Rukmini's worth?
qa.a: Recruiters may be busy or have delayed hiring, so silence can say more about their process than about her. The note does not say why.

grounding: A recruiter goes silent after promising a reply; the student follows up politely, keeps applying and does not read it as her worth.

passage:
Monday. Francis liked Samir's photo and, near midnight, sent "thinking of you 🙂". Samir smiled all through morning lectures. Then three days of nothing, until a meme arrived with no words.
Saturday. Samir noticed the pattern: warm bursts, never a plan. He wrote, "I'd like to actually meet this week. Would you?" Francis answered, "Ha, soon! Crazy busy right now."
Two weeks later. After another round of hearts and silence, Samir wrote, "I'm looking for someone who makes plans. I'll step back. Take care." His chest felt heavy, but he stopped checking his phone every hour, and on Sunday he went cycling with his friends.

qa.q: What did Francis send near midnight?
qa.a: Francis sent "thinking of you" with a smiling emoji.

qa.q: What did Samir feel on Monday morning, and what had changed by Saturday?
qa.a: He felt happy and hopeful and smiled all morning. By Saturday he saw that the warm messages never became plans, so he wanted a clear answer.

qa.q: Why was asking directly a good step for Samir?
qa.a: It gave Francis a chance to offer real plans and showed Samir what he was actually getting. When no plan came, he could step back instead of waiting for scraps.

qa.q: How might Francis see those messages?
qa.a: Francis may see them as friendly and casual rather than a promise, while Samir read them as hope. The vague "soon" shows Francis did not offer more.

grounding: Someone gives just enough attention to keep the protagonist hoping; he asks clearly and walks away when nothing is offered.

passage:
"I never said I'd pick you up," Farhan said. "You always twist things."
"You texted, 'I'll be there by six.' I have it right here."
"That was about the library. You're making it about you again. This is exactly why I get upset, Ganga."
Ganga opened her mouth, then closed it. "Sorry," she said, and hated that she had.
That night, at her sister's flat, she said, "Didi, this is the fourth time. I say what happened, he says it didn't, and I end up apologising."
"Do you write things down?"
"I've started. Dates, and what each of us said."
"Then keep going. That's not you being oversensitive. Come here more often and tell me what's happening."
Ganga nodded slowly. "It's not my fault. Is it?"
"It's not."

qa.q: What had Farhan texted Ganga?
qa.a: He had texted, "I'll be there by six."

qa.q: Why did Ganga say sorry even though she had the message?
qa.a: She felt confused and guilty, because Farhan turned the argument round until she seemed to be at fault. She hated apologising even as she did it.

qa.q: What could Ganga keep doing?
qa.a: She can keep her dated notes, keep talking to her sister and other trusted people outside the relationship, and trust her own memory of what happened.

qa.q: How does Ganga's sister see the situation?
qa.a: Didi sees a pattern in which Ganga's account is denied and she ends up apologising. She tells Ganga this is not oversensitivity and not her fault.

grounding: A partner twists the protagonist's words so she feels confused and guilty; she starts keeping notes and talks to her sister.

passage: Seema stood in the kitchen with her phone in her hand. Yesterday Jomon had promised to come to her cousin's wedding. Today he said, "I never said that. You imagine things. You're too sensitive." She remembered the exact evening, the kettle whistling, his nod. But the certainty was slipping, and that frightened her more than the argument. She opened a note on her phone and wrote the date, the place and what was said. Later she showed it to her friend Nandini, who frowned. "You told me about the wedding promise that same night." Seema breathed out. "So it did happen." Nandini nodded. "Every time he denies something, you end up doubting yourself instead of asking what he did. Maybe talk to the college counsellor." Seema booked a slot for the next morning.

qa.q: What did Jomon promise Seema the day before?
qa.a: He promised to come to her cousin's wedding.

qa.q: What frightened Seema more than the argument?
qa.a: She was frightened that her certainty was slipping and she was starting to doubt her own memory.

qa.q: What could Seema do next, besides the counsellor?
qa.a: She can keep dating her notes, keep checking things with trusted friends like Nandini, and notice whether the denials leave her doubting herself.

qa.q: How does Nandini see Jomon's denials?
qa.a: Nandini sees that each denial makes Seema doubt herself instead of asking what Jomon did, and she wants Seema to get support from a counsellor.

grounding: A partner denies events the protagonist clearly remembers and calls her oversensitive; she writes things down, checks with a friend and seeks counselling.

passage: I am Tenzin, and I want to tell you about last term, because I am still sorting it out. Binita and I were together nine months. Whenever I planned to see friends, she said, "If you go, I won't cope. I might do something to myself." The first time, I stayed home, shaking. By the third time I realised I was scared all the time, and that I could not be her only help. I did not laugh it off. I took what she said seriously. I told her older brother and the college counsellor together, so it was not just me carrying it. And I told Binita that I care about her, that she deserves proper support, but that I would not stop seeing my friends out of fear. She was furious and cried. It hurt. I am still worried about her.

qa.q: How long were Tenzin and Binita together?
qa.a: They were together nine months.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when Binita said she might do something to herself?
qa.a: Tenzin was scared. The first time Tenzin stayed home shaking, and later realised the fear had become constant.

qa.q: What was a wise part of how Tenzin responded?
qa.a: Tenzin took her words seriously and told her older brother and the counsellor rather than carrying it alone, while refusing to be controlled through fear. 🤍

qa.q: How might Binita have felt when Tenzin told others and set the limit?
qa.a: She was furious and cried, perhaps feeling exposed or afraid of being left. She may also be in real distress that needs proper support.

grounding: A partner threatens self-harm to stop the protagonist seeing friends; he takes it seriously, involves adults and professionals, and refuses control through fear.

passage: The first three weeks in Gothenburg were dizzying. Daniel met Lars outside every lecture with coffee, sent long messages at dawn, and said, "I have never met anyone like you. You are my whole world." Lars, far from home in his exchange year, felt chosen. Then one Thursday he said he needed an evening alone to finish an essay. Daniel's replies stopped. For four days there was nothing: no coffee, no messages, a blank chat under Lars's "Everything okay?" On Monday a bouquet arrived with a note: "Forgive me, I can't live without you." Lars held the flowers and noticed how his stomach felt, like a ship after a storm. He put them on the windowsill and wrote in his notebook: "Big gestures, then silence when I set a limit. What is he like on ordinary days?"

qa.q: How many days did Daniel go silent after Lars asked for an evening alone?
qa.a: Daniel was silent for four days.

qa.q: What does Lars's stomach feeling, like a ship after a storm, suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Lars felt unsettled and unsure, caught between the warmth of the first weeks and the sudden coldness.

qa.q: What should Lars watch for in the coming weeks?
qa.a: He can watch how Daniel behaves on ordinary days and when limits are set, and judge by steady behaviour rather than grand gestures. 🤍

qa.q: How might Daniel see the four days of silence?
qa.a: Daniel may feel hurt or rejected by the limit, which the note suggests. Still, the silence left Lars anxious, and that is what Lars is now weighing.

grounding: Intense adoration turns into silence when the protagonist sets a limit, and he notices the swing and looks to steady behaviour.

passage:
Nisha: Are you coming Saturday? Everyone's asking.
Hansa: I don't think so. Arohi gets upset when I go out without her.
Nisha: You've cancelled the last four things.
Hansa: I know. She says my friends don't really care about me and she's the only one who does. Some days I almost believe it.
Nisha: Han, we do care. I miss you.
Hansa: I miss you too. I've even stopped calling my mother as much because Arohi says it's clingy.
Nisha: That doesn't sound like you. Can I call you tomorrow, just us?
Hansa: Yes. Please.
Nisha: I'm here. Whenever you want.

qa.q: How many recent things has Hansa cancelled, according to Nisha?
qa.a: Nisha says Hansa has cancelled the last four things.

qa.q: What is Hansa feeling when writing that some days she almost believes Arohi?
qa.a: Hansa feels lonely and unsure, and has started to half-believe that only Arohi cares. Missing Nisha and her mother shows the pull the other way.

qa.q: What could Hansa do to keep an outside connection?
qa.a: She can accept Nisha's call, keep in touch with her mother and friends, and reach out to someone she trusts if the distance keeps growing.

qa.q: How does Nisha see Hansa's recent changes?
qa.a: Nisha notices the cancelled plans and says the change does not sound like Hansa. She misses her and offers a private call without judging.

grounding: A partner gradually distances the protagonist from friends and family; she keeps one outside connection by confiding in Nisha.

passage: On the way back from the temple fair, Yash walked three steps ahead of Aadhya and said nothing. She had told him she would go to the bangle stalls on Sunday with her cousins, without him. "Go, go," he said finally. "I'll sit at home alone. You never think of me." Aadhya's face fell. "Fine, I'll stay," she said. Yash felt a small win, and then something hollow underneath. He had seen her eyes fill. That night, sitting on the charpai, he asked himself what he was so afraid of, and the answer came out plain: that she would have a better time without him. Two days later he said, "Aadhya, can I come on Sunday? If not, I'll manage." She thought a moment. "Not this Sunday. Next fair, together." Yash swallowed. "Okay," he said, and it felt harder and cleaner than sulking.

qa.q: Where were Yash and Aadhya coming back from?
qa.a: They were coming back from the temple fair.

qa.q: What did Yash feel after Aadhya said she would stay?
qa.a: He felt a small win and then something hollow. He had seen her eyes fill, and he later admitted he feared she would have a better time without him.

qa.q: What could Yash do next time he feels left out?
qa.a: He can ask directly, as he did in the end, accept a no, and talk about the fear of being left behind instead of using guilt or sulking.

qa.q: How does Aadhya see the sulking on the walk back?
qa.a: Aadhya felt hurt, since her face fell and her eyes filled, and she gave up her plan to keep the peace. Her later no shows she still wants time with her cousins.

grounding: The protagonist uses guilt and sulking to get his way, then sees the fear behind it and asks directly and accepts a no.

passage: Lokesh waited forty minutes at the kasba bus stand because Baljeet's tailoring class had run late. When she stepped off, he was already asking: who had she sat with, why hadn't she texted, whose phone was that. "It's love," he said. "I only worry because I care." She looked tired, not touched. That night on the roof Lokesh went over it. He had been reading her messages for weeks. What he felt was not care, he admitted, it was a fear that she would leave. The next day he told his friend Gopal, who listened and did not laugh. On Sunday he went with Gopal to the youth counsellor at the block office. Then he told Baljeet, "I've been holding on too tight. I'm going to talk to someone about it, and I'll stop checking your phone."

qa.q: How long did Lokesh wait at the bus stand?
qa.a: He waited forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Lokesh really feeling beneath his questions at the bus stand?
qa.a: He realised that what he felt was not care but fear that Baljeet would leave, and that he had been reading her messages out of that fear.

qa.q: What could Lokesh do to keep making progress?
qa.a: He can keep seeing the counsellor, keep talking with Gopal, and practise trusting Baljeet without checking her phone or questioning her.

qa.q: How did Baljeet likely feel at the bus stand?
qa.a: She looked tired, not touched, so the questions probably felt heavy rather than loving. Calling it love did not change how it landed for her.

grounding: The protagonist controls his partner out of fear of abandonment, then admits it, seeks a counsellor and lets go of control.

passage: Rajni had fifteen minutes of lunch break, and she spent them in the office stairwell with the phone against her ear, whispering to a helpline volunteer. Vishal was collecting her from work at six, as he always did. Her heart thudded at every footstep. "I don't know if I'm brave enough," she said. "And what will Papa say? And who do I have here?" The volunteer did not hurry her. "You are not weak for wanting to leave. Let's think about a safe plan, with someone you trust." Rajni named her friend Kavya. That evening she carried on as usual. Later she sent Kavya one message: "Can we talk tomorrow? I need help." Kavya wrote back, "Yes. Any time. I'm here." Rajni held the phone to her chest, afraid, but no longer alone.

qa.q: Where did Rajni make her call?
qa.a: She made the call in the office stairwell.

qa.q: What is Rajni afraid of when she says she doesn't know if she is brave enough?
qa.a: She fears Vishal, being lonely with no one nearby, and her father's reaction. She wonders whether she can face all three.

qa.q: What should Rajni do next?
qa.a: She can talk with Kavya, keep working with the helpline volunteer on a safe plan, and put safety first before deciding how and when. 🤍

qa.q: How might Kavya feel receiving Rajni's message?
qa.a: Kavya was ready to help straight away, replying "Yes. Any time. I'm here." She likely feels concerned and glad Rajni trusted her.

grounding: The protagonist wants to leave a toxic partner but fears him, loneliness and family reaction, and plans with a helpline and a friend.
